title: Tamiflu isn't over the counter: how to get it from a doctor online
summary: Tamiflu isn't over the counter in the US. See CDC antiviral rules, the 48-hour window, generic oseltamivir and Xofluza prices, and online doctor options.
body_markdown:
In the United States, Tamiflu (oseltamivir) and other flu antivirals require a prescription. On its[flu treatment page](https://www.cdc.gov/flu/treatment/index.html) (read October 2026), the CDC states: "Antiviral drugs are not sold over the counter," and "You can only get them from a pharmacy if you have a prescription." Every FDA oseltamivir and baloxavir label (as of October 2026) reads "HUMAN PRESCRIPTION DRUG."


In its[antiviral summary for clinicians](https://www.cdc.gov/flu/hcp/antivirals/summary-clinicians.html) (dated March 10, 2026, read October 2026), the CDC notes that "Clinicians can utilize telemedicine in place of office visits" for acute respiratory illness. On[FutureClinic](https://futureclinic.com/) , every clinician is a state-licensed physician with an MD, DO or MBBS degree, never a nurse practitioner or physician assistant. A specific doctor reads your whole case and answers with a written plan and a Human Signature, a short video or voice note recorded live for you. No form is approved in bulk. Replies typically come within a few hours, and almost always the same day or the next, so start when symptoms begin. FutureClinic is not for emergencies: for emergency warning signs, go in person to an emergency room or call 911, or call or text 988 in a mental-health crisis.


Is it another service with its extra requirements you want, or a doctor who answers you? On FutureClinic, the same doctor can help with other problems in their specialty, and every FutureClinic doctor you see works from one medical record.


## Who should take a flu antiviral and why the 48-hour window matters


Flu brings sudden fever or chills, cough, sore throat, runny nose, body aches, headaches and fatigue. Mild flu usually resolves in under two weeks without antivirals, and antibiotics never treat viruses.


The CDC recommends four FDA-approved, non-controlled antivirals: oral oseltamivir (Tamiflu and generic), oral baloxavir (Xofluza), inhaled zanamivir (Relenza, from age 7, not for asthma or COPD), and IV peramivir (Rapivab, an in-person infusion). Under CDC guidance and[IDSA guidelines](https://www.idsociety.org/practice-guideline/influenza/) , treatment should start as soon as possible for patients who are hospitalized, have severe or worsening illness, or are at[higher risk for flu complications](https://www.cdc.gov/flu/highrisk/index.htm) : adults 65 and older, children under 5 (especially under 2), pregnant people (up to 2 weeks post-pregnancy), nursing-home residents, and those with asthma, chronic lung, heart, kidney, liver, blood, metabolic or neurologic conditions, diabetes, a BMI of 40 or higher, or weakened immunity. The CDC states treatment in priority groups "should not wait for laboratory confirmation of influenza virus infection."


Healthy outpatients can also be considered for treatment within 48 hours of symptom onset, including by telemedicine. Starting within two days works best and can "shorten the time you are sick by about a day," per the CDC. In adult trials on the[Tamiflu FDA label](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/search.cfm?labeltype=all&query=oseltamivir) (ages 18 to 65, started within 40 hours), median time to improvement was 1.3 days shorter than with placebo. Still, the CDC notes "starting them later can still be helpful" for higher-risk, worsening or hospitalized patients.


## Generic Tamiflu vs Xofluza: doses, side effects and October 2026 cash prices


In a[March 20, 2026 update](https://www.cdc.gov/flu/whats-new/2025-2026-underutilization-of-flu-antivirals.html) , the CDC called oral oseltamivir "the default option for most patients with flu," including in pregnancy. Approved from age 2 weeks, the adult and teen (13+) treatment dose is 75 mg twice daily for 5 days (10 capsules), with weight-based children's dosing and renal adjustments. Baloxavir (Xofluza) is a single tablet (40 mg for 20 to under 80 kg; 80 mg for 80 kg or more) approved from age 5, though not recommended alone for pregnant or breastfeeding, immunocompromised, worsening or hospitalized patients. On the[Xofluza FDA label](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/search.cfm?labeltype=all&query=baloxavir) , healthy patients 12 and older reached symptom relief in a median of 54 hours on Xofluza or oseltamivir versus 80 hours on placebo. Avoid taking Xofluza with dairy, calcium-fortified drinks, mineral antacids or laxatives, or calcium, iron, magnesium, selenium or zinc supplements.


In adult Tamiflu trials, nausea (10% vs 6% on placebo), vomiting (8% vs 3%) and headache were the top side effects; food helps, and nausea usually passes in two days. Rare serious skin reactions and rare delirium or abnormal behavior (mostly in children) appear on the label. In Xofluza trials (ages 12+), diarrhea (3%), bronchitis (3%), nausea (2%), sinusitis (2%) and headache (1%) were no more common than with placebo.


As of October 2026, cash prices are:


-


**Generic oseltamivir:** On the[Cost Plus Drugs price list](https://api.costplusdrugs.com/pricelist/cpd) (as of October 2026), ten 75 mg capsules cost $12.88 before shipping ($18.13 shipped); 45 mg costs $8.25 ($13.50 shipped) and 30 mg costs $8.33 ($13.58 shipped).


-


**Brand Xofluza:** Cost Plus Drugs lists one 40 mg or 80 mg tablet at $183.93 before shipping ($189.18 shipped) as of October 2026. Through[Genentech's self-pay program](https://www.gene.com/media/press-releases/15081/2025-10-16/genentech-expands-xofluza-access-and-aff) and[Xofluza coupon page](https://www.xofluza.com/coupon.html) (as of October 2026), eligible uninsured self-pay patients pay a $50 flat fee via select pharmacies (Alto Pharmacy, Cost Plus Drugs, and Costco for members), or as little as $35 (up to $70 off) with a coupon at most pharmacies for commercially insured or cash-paying patients (excluding Medicare, Medicaid and TRICARE).


If your doctor decides it's right for you, FutureClinic sends prescriptions to the pharmacy you choose, including local or mail-order pharmacies that deliver to your door, with a cash discount coupon, or you can use insurance at the pharmacy. FutureClinic also helps get prior authorizations when insurance requires one.
